title: How ideas become knowledge

nodes.label: How ideas become knowledge
nodes.description: This original demonstration describes a careful reading practice: begin with a question, preserve the source, organise ideas, examine arguments, explain connections and revise interpretations.

nodes.label: Begin with curiosity
nodes.description: A useful inquiry starts with a question specific enough to investigate and open enough to change.

nodes.label: Ask a useful question
nodes.description: A useful question names what is uncertain instead of disguising a preferred answer as a question.

nodes.label: Name your purpose
nodes.description: The purpose of an inquiry might be to understand, compare, explain, decide or design.

nodes.label: Set the boundary
nodes.description: A boundary names the time, place, people and material that an inquiry will cover.

nodes.label: Notice surprises
nodes.description: An observation that does not fit an expectation can become the beginning of a new question.

nodes.label: Keep an open notebook
nodes.description: A notebook can preserve initial questions so that later answers do not erase how the inquiry began.

nodes.label: Make uncertainty visible
nodes.description: Writing “I do not know yet” keeps an unanswered question distinct from a confident conclusion.

nodes.label: Gather with care
nodes.description: Gathering material includes recording where it came from, what it covers and what it leaves out.

nodes.label: Preserve the source
nodes.description: Keep a source passage in its original form so that a later interpretation can be checked against it.

nodes.label: Record the location
nodes.description: A page, paragraph or timestamp makes a claim easier to find in the original material.

nodes.label: Distinguish voices
nodes.description: Separate what a source author says from what a quoted speaker or later reader says.

nodes.label: Mark missing context
nodes.description: An excerpt may omit qualifications that appear elsewhere, so its boundary belongs beside its analysis.

nodes.label: Keep contradictions
nodes.description: Sources that disagree should retain their separate claims and attribution until the disagreement is examined.

nodes.label: A quotation is an anchor
nodes.description: A quotation shows what a source says; it does not by itself establish that the statement is true.

nodes.label: Give ideas a shape
nodes.description: A mind map arranges ideas into a readable hierarchy while a knowledge graph records relationships across that hierarchy.

nodes.label: Find the central question
nodes.description: The root of a map should give the reader a clear account of the inquiry being explored.

nodes.label: Name the main themes
nodes.description: Major branches should reflect the material rather than a template imposed on every source.

nodes.label: Define concepts in context
nodes.description: A definition should explain how a term is being used in this particular material.

nodes.label: Connect across branches
nodes.description: A cross-link can show that an idea in one branch supports, challenges or depends on an idea elsewhere.

nodes.label: Preserve different meanings
nodes.description: Two passages using the same word can express different concepts and should not be merged merely because their labels match.

nodes.label: Maps are interpretations
nodes.description: Grouping an idea under a heading is an editorial choice, even when the idea itself is directly quoted.

nodes.label: Examine the argument
nodes.description: Examining an argument means separating its claims, evidence, assumptions and possible objections.

nodes.label: Find the claim
nodes.description: A claim is a statement the source asks its reader to accept.

nodes.label: Inspect the support
nodes.description: Support may include observations, measurements, examples, testimony or reasoning; these play different roles.

nodes.label: Surface assumptions
nodes.description: An assumption connects steps in an argument without always being stated directly.

nodes.label: Consider another reading
nodes.description: An alternative interpretation can expose an ambiguity without proving the original interpretation wrong.

nodes.label: Respect causal limits
nodes.description: An association between two observations does not by itself identify a causal mechanism.

nodes.label: Ask what would change your mind
nodes.description: A claim becomes easier to examine when the reader can name evidence that would count against it.

nodes.label: Make understanding useful
nodes.description: An explanation becomes useful when another person can follow its structure and inspect its support.

nodes.label: Explain in plain language
nodes.description: Clear language lets a reader spend attention on the idea instead of decoding unnecessary jargon.

nodes.label: Teach the connections
nodes.description: A teaching outline should show why ideas connect as well as what each idea means.

nodes.label: Make a concrete example
nodes.description: An example can illustrate an idea, while its limits prevent the example from standing in for every case.

nodes.label: Turn questions into practice
nodes.description: A study question can ask a learner to compare, explain or apply an idea rather than only repeat a label.

nodes.label: Keep evidence within reach
nodes.description: A reader should be able to move from a compact map label to its explanation and source passage.

nodes.label: Offer more than one view
nodes.description: A text outline and a visual map can describe the same structure for readers with different needs.

nodes.label: Leave room to revise
nodes.description: A knowledge map remains useful when it records uncertainty and can change as new material arrives.

nodes.label: Label interpretations
nodes.description: An inferred connection should identify the passages and reasoning that motivated it.

nodes.label: Separate possibilities
nodes.description: A speculative possibility belongs in an exploratory layer, apart from what the source explicitly states.

nodes.label: Keep open questions
nodes.description: An unresolved question can identify a productive next step without pretending that the source supplied an answer.

nodes.label: Review a changed source
nodes.description: When the source changes, check the interpretations and quotations that depended on its earlier wording.

nodes.label: Save an editable version
nodes.description: An editable version preserves the structure needed to revise a map beyond its exported picture.

nodes.label: Learning is revisable
nodes.description: A revision should make clear what changed and why, so that a polished map does not hide its uncertainty.

edges.rationale: Preserved passages let a reader inspect what is offered as support.
Recorded locations let a reader return from an explanation to its source.
Cross-links make connections available for teaching.
Recognising assumptions and labelling interpretation are complementary reading practices.
Preserving disagreement keeps alternative readings available for examination.
An initial question and an unresolved question both make uncertainty visible.
An editable map gives the reader a way to revise source-dependent interpretations.
Both passages limit what can be concluded from an observation or quotation.
